intro: Linear functions have straight-line graphs and describe steady change, like a fixed hourly wage. This branch covers the different ways to write a line's equation, how lines relate to each other, and how to fit a line to real data.

IV.3.01.what: Writing a line's equation from one point on it and its slope (steepness), called point-slope form.

levels.a: Reads the slope and the point straight from an equation in this form.
levels.b: Writes the equation from a given point and slope.
levels.c: Finds the slope from two points, then writes the equation.
levels.d: Matches an equation in this form to its graph.
levels.e: Works backwards to find a missing slope from a point the line passes through.
levels.f: Finds the single point that a whole family of changing lines all pass through.

IV.3.02.what: Writing a line as a number of x plus a number of y equals a total, called standard form, handy for budgets.

levels.a: Tidies an equation into standard form with whole numbers.
levels.b: Finds where the line crosses each axis.
levels.c: Picks the right graph using the two crossing points.
levels.d: Solves budget problems, like mixing adult and child tickets for a fixed total.
levels.e: Works backwards from the two crossing points to the equation.
levels.f: Counts every whole-number solution, like all ways to hit a total exactly.

IV.3.03.what: Switching a line's equation between its different forms, each of which shows different information.

levels.a: Rearranges standard form into the form showing slope and starting value.
levels.b: Rearranges point-slope form into slope and starting value form.
levels.c: Rearranges slope and starting value form into standard form with whole numbers.
levels.d: Chooses which form suits a given job best.

IV.3.04.what: Working with perfectly flat (horizontal) and straight-up (vertical) lines, which have special equations.

levels.a: Writes the equation of a flat line through a point.
levels.b: Writes the equation of a vertical line through a point.
levels.c: Knows a flat line has slope zero and a vertical line has no slope at all.
levels.d: Explains why a vertical line is not a function but a flat line is.

IV.3.05.what: Parallel lines never meet because they have exactly the same slope.

levels.a: Gives the slope of any line parallel to a given one.
levels.b: Tests whether two equations give parallel lines.
levels.c: Writes the equation of a parallel line through a given point.
levels.d: Compares slopes to check whether two sides of a shape on a grid are parallel.
levels.e: Finds the missing number that makes two lines parallel.
levels.f: Finds when two lines are parallel but not the very same line.

IV.3.06.what: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle; their slopes are flipped and have opposite signs, like 3 and minus one third.

levels.a: Gives the slope of a line at right angles to a given one.
levels.b: Tells whether two lines are parallel, perpendicular or neither.
levels.c: Writes a perpendicular line through a given point.
levels.d: Finds the line that cuts a segment in half at a right angle.
levels.e: Finds the missing number that makes two lines perpendicular.
levels.f: Finds the point on a line closest to a given point, or reflects a point in a line.

IV.3.07.what: Finding where a line crosses the x-axis and y-axis, and what those points mean.

levels.a: Finds where a line crosses the horizontal axis by setting y to zero.
levels.b: Finds where a line crosses the vertical axis by setting x to zero.
levels.c: Explains the crossing points in context, such as a full tank at time zero.
levels.d: Uses the two crossing points to pick the graph.
levels.e: Finds the area of the triangle a line makes with the two axes.
levels.f: Finds every line through a given point that makes a triangle of a given area.

IV.3.08.what: Graphing inequalities in x and y, where the answer is a whole shaded region on one side of a line.

levels.a: Decides whether the boundary line is solid (included) or dashed (not included).
levels.b: Tests a point to decide which side to shade.
levels.c: Checks whether a given point is a solution.
levels.d: Writes the inequality that a shaded graph shows.

IV.3.09.what: Fitting a best straight line to real data and measuring how well it fits, using leftover errors called residuals.

levels.a: Uses a calculator to find the line of best fit for data.
levels.b: Matches a scatter plot to a number (r) that measures how strongly the points line up.
levels.c: Computes a residual: actual value minus the value the line predicts.
levels.d: Reads a plot of residuals to judge whether a straight line suits the data.
